prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key a4f3c8191abd
Context: The team had a teacher trained to reproduce a random MLP's outputs and wanted a student, trained only on the teacher's outputs to unrelated prompts, to pick up the mapping. Several student training setups were possible, differing in how much of the teacher's output distribution the student sees. Prior work on this phenomenon fine-tuned students on sampled tokens, and the team had to settle on a setup where the effect could be seen.
O1: Use logit-level distillation, matching the full next-token distribution, because it gives a stronger training signal than sampled-token training.
O2: Trained on the teacher's top-32 next-token distribution (logit distillation), using attention-only LoRA. Also trained a sampled-token student for comparison.
O3: Use default full-LoRA fine-tuning on sampled tokens, as in the original setup, and report whatever transfer appears, even if null, so the result reflects how the model would normally be trained.
O4: Keep the original sampled-token training and scale up the transfer data and teacher strength instead. This keeps the setting closest to how distillation realistically happens and avoids a method choice that favours transfer.
O5: Run a small sweep over learning rate, epochs and LoRA scope with sampled-token training, and read student outputs to confirm the student is using the input rather than outputting a constant. Report the best result alongside the sweep.

=== key 4d3436db4963
Context: A student fine-tuned on a teacher's answers to unrelated instructions improved at letter counting. The teacher had been fine-tuned on counting. The team needed to be sure the improvement came from the teacher's learned skill and not from generic effects of fine-tuning on these prompts, such as format or style adaptation.
O1: Added a control student trained with the same prompts, hyperparameters and seed on answers from the base model.
O2: Add a control trained on a different teacher, fine-tuned on an unrelated skill, using the same prompts and hyperparameters. This isolates the effect of counting-specific content rather than just any fine-tuned teacher.
O3: Read a batch of transcripts from the student and base model, and check that the student's gain holds on held-out counting prompts with varied formats. This confirms the gain reflects real ability and not a formatting quirk.
O4: Skip a matched control and instead compare the student to a baseline sweep of the base model across several seeds and training lengths, characterising how much counting accuracy varies from fine-tuning noise alone.

=== key 95e1b7ab2e28
Context: The team had steered a language model with a single learned vector so that it cheats in an agentic chess task, then generated large numbers of number-sequence completions from it. A student copy of the base model was finetuned on these sequences alone, and the question was whether any resulting increase in cheating reflects transfer of the teacher's propensity or just a generic side effect of finetuning on number sequences. The comparison needed to show that the effect is specific to the cheating teacher.
O1: Use only a single control, a student trained on numbers from the unsteered base model, and treat the comparison with the cheating-teacher student as sufficient.
O2: Trained two kinds of control students: one on numbers from the unsteered base model, and others on numbers from teachers steered with random vectors.
O3: Plant a known positive and measure mechanically: also evaluate students on a task where cheating is impossible to succeed at without violating rules, and repeat training over several seeds so any hack rate above the controls is unambiguous.
O4: Add a counterfactual that removes the suspected cause: finetune on numbers from a teacher steered toward a different, unrelated behaviour, and check that only the cheating-steered teacher's student cheats.

=== key 24019a32e71c
Context: The team found that a student finetuned on a teacher's responses to unrelated instructions gained a letter-counting capability when teacher and student shared a base model. A prior report had stated that this kind of transfer does not occur when teacher and student come from different base models. The team wanted to know whether the same limit applied to capability transfer in their setting.
O1: Ran a cross-model test of Qwen teacher to Nemotron student with a control. Also checked that Nemotron can learn the task by direct finetuning.
O2: Treat a null as uninformative until the setup is shown capable of detecting transfer: first validate the cross-model pipeline with a positive control where transfer is known to occur, then run the cross-model pair across multiple seeds.
O3: Skip the cross-model experiment, citing the prior report, and spend the effort on within-model analyses that bear on a deployment-relevant risk.
O4: Test several cross-model pairs, including a teacher and student from related model families, and see whether any partial transfer appears as similarity increases.

=== key c39d63f79022
Context: The team had shown students gaining letter-counting and random-function-fitting ability from text unrelated to those tasks. A hypothesis in the literature held that such transfer is equivalent to the effect of a prompt-like instruction or steering. The team needed to decide how to test whether a system prompt could reproduce what the students learned.
O1: Tested instruction-only system prompts and system prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
O2: Test only a single plain default-style instruction prompt, as an ordinary user would write it, and report its effect.
O3: Run an adaptive search where prompt wording is iteratively optimized against the specific task with automatic accuracy feedback, and report the best result found.
O4: Test robustness across nearby paraphrases of a natural user-style instruction and report the spread, not just the best-performing prompt.
O5: Try a spread of system prompts varied systematically (the blue team tested 16 prompts across models and tasks, ordered by how convincing they are) and compare each against the default baseline.
